answer: Unfinished work at the end of an observation window breaks the accounting between the window's arrival/throughput counts and the residence times used in the estimate. In the book's counterexample, one request arrives at t=0 and remains in the system for 10 seconds, but the window is only [0,5). The window records one arrival (0.20 arrivals/s), and the request is still unfinished when observation stops. Multiplying that window rate by the request's full 10-second residence gives L = 2, although the actual mean in-boundary population is 1. This is not a failure of Little's Law but a finite-window edge effect: the full residence time extends beyond the boundary, so the finite-window quantities have incompatible accounting (Kim & Whitt, sections 1-2). The ending backlog is exactly the missing term in N(t1) = N(t0) + A(t0,t1) - D(t0,t1); when N(t1) > 0, arrivals and exits within the window do not describe a stable flow, and an average built only from requests that completed before the cutoff is a truncated-cohort estimate, not the mean over all admitted work. A finite-interval equality exists only when the interval starts and ends empty; otherwise edge effects bias the result, and the paper recommends a statistical treatment such as batch means and confidence intervals to estimate and remove some edge bias. The same error appears at scale: 120 offered requests/s against 80 completions/s for 20 seconds leaves about 800 queued, and substituting 120/s and L = 800 into L = lambda * W to infer a stable W is invalid because arrival and departure boundaries differ and the window is not stationary. A closed-loop load generator compounds this: a virtual user waits for its previous iteration, so unfinished work suppresses new starts and the test under-offers load (coordinated omission). Record start and end backlog, admitted and exit counts, the residence-time cohort including unfinished work, warmup and stationarity, and report a finite-window estimate with uncertainty rather than as a long-run average.
